title: What is jQuery?
summary: Introduces jQuery as the most widely used JavaScript library and shows why it exists: it collapses verbose DOM code into short expressions such as $("h1"). It also notes that a library is simply someone else's code you pull into your project, like Bootstrap.

concepts.heading: What a library is
points: A library is a bundle of code written by someone else that you include in your project to save effort. Bootstrap, used earlier for CSS/JS components, is the same idea.
jQuery was created by John Resig because plain DOM scripting felt long-winded for simple jobs. It became the most downloaded JavaScript library.
Later sections of the course meet other libraries too, so this is the first example of a pattern: add a library, then call its functions.

concepts.heading: The problem jQuery solves
points: The comparison example is a drum-kit style snippet: query all buttons, loop over them with a for loop, attach a click listener to each, and inside the callback query the h1 and set its style.color to red.
In plain JavaScript each step needs its own call (querySelectorAll, loop, addEventListener, querySelector, .style.color), so a trivial behaviour takes many lines.
jQuery condenses the selecting, looping over matches and event wiring into a few short calls, so code is quicker to write, easier to read and easier to debug.

concepts.heading: The jQuery function and the $ shorthand
points: jQuery("h1") looks up elements by a CSS selector, much as document.querySelector("h1") does.
$ is a shorthand alias for jQuery, so $("h1") and jQuery("h1") are identical.
(Extra) Unlike querySelector, the jQuery selection can hold many elements and methods called on it apply to all of them, which is why the explicit for loop disappears.

code_examples.caption: Plain JavaScript version: listener on every button, turns the h1 red
Selecting an element: vanilla vs jQuery
code_examples.code:
document.querySelector("h1");   // vanilla
jQuery("h1");                   // full name
$("h1");                        // shorthand, same thing

pitfalls: jQuery code only works once the library has been loaded into the page; otherwise $ is undefined (covered in the next lecture).

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'jQuery: less code for the same DOM job'. Blurb: compare vanilla DOM scripting with jQuery. Tasks: (1) write the vanilla loop-plus-listener that colours the h1; (2) rewrite it with $(...); (3) count the lines and characters of each; (4) note which version is easier to read. Starter code: three buttons and an h1. Interactive demo: side-by-side panes running both versions on the same buttons.
